title: Project life cycles
exam_coverage_note: 4 of 60 marks. One exam question per learning outcome.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 1.2.2, 1.2.3, 1.2.4, 1.2.5 and 8th ed. 2.5.1, 2.5.2, 2.5.3, 2.5.4.
competence_area_note: The handbook publishes no per-objective Competence Framework mapping. Left null rather than guessed.
where_this_fits: Four marks sit here. The life cycle is the first structural decision made on a project, and the rest of the course assumes you can tell the types apart. Learn the four linear phases as one phrase, then learn what makes iterative, hybrid and extended different.

key_definitions.definition: The series of distinct phases a project passes through, from initial idea to completion, providing a structure for managing and controlling the work.
key_definitions.plain_english: The stages a project moves through from start to finish. The skeleton everything else hangs on.

key_definitions.definition: A life cycle in which the phases run once, in sequence, with scope defined before delivery begins.
key_definitions.plain_english: Plan it fully, then build it. Changes afterwards go through change control.

key_definitions.definition: A life cycle in which development repeats in cycles, with requirements refined and re-prioritised as the work progresses.
key_definitions.plain_english: Build a bit, show it, learn from it, build the next bit.

key_definitions.definition: A life cycle combining elements of the linear and iterative approaches within a single project.
key_definitions.plain_english: Fixed and planned at the front, iterative in delivery. Both, in one project.

key_definitions.definition: A life cycle that adds adoption and benefits realisation phases after the phases of a linear life cycle.
key_definitions.plain_english: The project is not finished when the output is handed over. It is finished when the benefits arrive.

core_content.outcome_title: State the phases of a typical linear project life cycle
core_content.key_takeaway: A linear project life cycle has four phases: concept, definition, deployment, transition. Concept establishes the need, definition works out how the project will be done, deployment produces the outputs, and transition hands them over and closes the project down. The full scope is agreed before delivery starts. Deployment is normally the longest and most expensive phase, which is why concept and definition exist to test the idea cheaply first. Feasibility is an activity carried out within concept, not a phase in its own right. Decision gates sit between the phases.
core_content.body_markdown:
Concept establishes the need. Is there a problem worth solving, and is this idea worth pursuing at all? Work here is deliberately cheap, because most ideas examined at concept should never go further.

Definition works out how the project will be done. Scope, schedule, cost, risk and quality are settled, and the project management plan is produced. By the end of definition the organisation knows what it is committing to.

Deployment is where the work happens and the outputs are produced. This is normally the longest and most expensive phase, which is exactly why the two phases before it exist.

Transition hands the outputs over to the people who will use them, and the temporary project structure is dissolved.

The word linear is doing real work. The phases run once, in order, and the full scope is agreed before delivery starts. Because scope was fixed up front, any change to it later has to be formally requested, assessed and approved.

Between the phases sit decision gates. A gate is where the organisation decides whether the project should carry on at all, based on whether the business case still holds.

core_content.outcome_title: State the phases of a typical iterative project life cycle
core_content.key_takeaway: An iterative life cycle has concept, definition, development and deployment, with development repeating. Each development iteration produces something usable, and user feedback shapes the next one. It is used when the requirements cannot be specified precisely at the start.
core_content.body_markdown:
An iterative life cycle still begins with concept and definition. What changes is that the single run through delivery is replaced by repeated development iterations, each producing something usable.

The reason to work this way is uncertainty about requirements. If nobody can say precisely what is needed at the start, defining the whole scope in advance produces a confident plan for the wrong thing. Iterating builds a small piece, puts it in front of users, and lets their response shape what comes next.

What is deferred is the detail, not the planning. There is still a concept phase and still a definition phase. The high level scope, the budget and the overall objectives are still agreed up front.

Time and resources are fixed for each iteration, and the scope flexes to fit. That is what stops an iterative project running forever.

core_content.key_takeaway: A hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative elements within a single project. A common pattern is a linear concept and definition, with a fixed business case and budget, followed by iterative delivery inside those boundaries. The organisation gains financial control and governance from the linear part, and the delivery team gains a feedback loop from the iterative part.
core_content.body_markdown:
A hybrid takes what each approach is good at.

The usual pattern is a linear front end, with a fixed concept, an agreed business case and an agreed budget, followed by iterative delivery inside those boundaries. The organisation gets the financial control and governance it needs, and the team gets the feedback loop it needs.

Hybrids also appear where different parts of one project have different characteristics. Constructing a building is not sensibly done in iterations, but the software controlling it might be. One project, two approaches, each chosen to suit the work.

For the exam the definition is all that is needed. Hybrid means both, in one project.

core_content.outcome_title: Define the term 'extended project life cycle'
core_content.key_takeaway: An extended project life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after the phases of a linear life cycle. Adoption is the period when people start using the output properly. Benefits realisation is the period when the expected improvement is measured and confirmed.
core_content.body_markdown:
If the purpose of project management is beneficial change, a project that hands over its output and stops has not necessarily delivered anything of value. A new system nobody uses produces no benefit at all, however well it was built.

Adoption is the period during which the people who received the output actually start using it, and using it properly. Training, support and behaviour change sit here.

Benefits realisation is the period during which the expected improvement is measured and confirmed.

Extending the life cycle changes who is answerable. Under a standard linear life cycle the project ends at transition, and whether benefits appear becomes somebody else's problem. Under an extended life cycle someone stays accountable until they do.

misconceptions.wrong: Iterative is the modern approach and is therefore better.
misconceptions.right: Neither is better. Each suits different conditions. Linear suits work where requirements are knowable up front and change is expensive. Iterative suits work where requirements emerge and feedback is cheap.

misconceptions.wrong: Iterative projects have no planning phase.
misconceptions.right: They have both concept and definition. The high-level scope, budget and objectives are agreed up front. Only the detail is settled iteration by iteration.

misconceptions.wrong: Hybrid and extended are two names for the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Hybrid combines linear and iterative approaches. Extended adds adoption and benefits realisation after handover. They answer entirely different questions.

misconceptions.wrong: Feasibility is a phase of the linear life cycle.
misconceptions.right: Feasibility is an activity carried out within the concept phase. The four phases are concept, definition, deployment, transition.

misconceptions.wrong: The project is finished once the output is handed over.
misconceptions.right: Under a standard linear life cycle, yes. Under an extended life cycle the project remains accountable through adoption and benefits realisation.

misconceptions.wrong: Choosing a life cycle is a technical decision for the delivery team.
misconceptions.right: It determines how scope, baselines, change control, governance and reviews all work. It is the first structural decision on the project and it reaches into most of the rest of the syllabus.

memory_aids.expansion: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. The four linear phases, in order. If you learn one list in this objective, learn this one.
Hybrid mixes approaches. Extended extends past handover. Two words that separate the most confused pair in the objective.
Linear fixes scope and flexes time and cost. Iterative fixes time and cost and flexes scope. Almost every linear versus iterative question reduces to this.
A standard life cycle ends at handover. An extended one ends when the benefit lands.

progress_checkpoint: I can recite the four phases of a linear life cycle in order, without pausing.
I can say what happens in each of those four phases in one sentence.
I can name the phases of an iterative life cycle and say which one repeats.
I can explain what is fixed and what flexes in linear work, and in iterative work.
I can define a hybrid life cycle and distinguish it from an extended one.
I can define an extended life cycle and name the two phases it adds.

source_confidence.claim: The four phases of a typical linear life cycle are concept, definition, deployment, transition.
source_confidence.basis: Syllabus outcome 2.1 with APM Body of Knowledge references; corroborated by the published PFQ sample paper, which tests this sequence directly.
source_confidence.risk: Some training providers teach a five-phase variant that separates handover from closure. The four-phase sequence is what the PFQ syllabus and sample paper use, and that is what we teach.

source_confidence.claim: Development is the phase that distinguishes an iterative life cycle from a linear one.
source_confidence.basis: Derived from the syllabus outcome and the sample paper item on iterative phases, which excludes concept and feasibility from the correct answer.
source_confidence.risk: The sample paper is dated 2022 and predates Body of Knowledge 8th edition. If APM restates iterative phases in a revised syllabus, this outcome should be re-checked before relying on the distinction.
